The problem is that `middle_unescaped` and `middle` have different lengths when HTML entities are present. When we compute `middle[len(stripped):]`, we're using the length from the unescaped string to index into the escaped string.


Let me trace through a concrete example to see exactly where this breaks down. With `google.com/?q=1&lt!`, after unescaping I get `google.com/?q=1<!`. When I strip the trailing punctuation, the `!` gets removed leaving `google.com/?q=1<`. But now I'm using the length of that stripped string (17) to slice back into the original escaped string, which pulls out `t!` instead of just `!`.

The real problem is that I'm mixing lengths from the unescaped domain with indices into the escaped string. I need to figure out which characters in the escaped version correspond to the trailing characters in the unescaped version, then work backwards from there. of trailing characters stripped from the unescaped string is `len(middle_unescaped) - len(stripped)`.

Now we need to figure out what portion of `middle` (escaped) corresponds to those trailing characters. The key insight is that the trailing punctuation characters (`.,:;!`) are never part of HTML entities, so each stripped character from the unescaped version corresponds exactly to one character in the escaped version.

Wait, let me verify: the TRAILING_PUNCTUATION_CHARS are `.,:;!`. The semicolons `;` could be part of HTML entities. But the comment says "Unescape entities to avoid breaking them by removing ';'". So the unescaping is done precisely to handle the case where `;` at the end of an entity shouldn't be stripped.

After unescaping, if we strip trailing punctuation, those characters in the unescaped string are actual punctuation, not parts of entities. Since they're plain characters (`.,:;!`), they map 1:1 in the escaped string as well. So I should strip the same number of trailing characters from `middle` as I removed from `middle_unescaped`. Working through the example: if I stripped 1 character from the unescaped version, I remove 1 character from the end of `middle` and prepend it to the trailing punctuation. I'm tracing through the indexing more carefully—when I use a negative index like `middle[:-1]`, it removes the last character, so `google.com/?q=1&lt!` becomes `google.com/?q=1&lt`, which is 19 characters instead of 20.

But then for the trail calculation, I'm indexing into `middle` using `len(stripped)` which is measured in unescaped characters, not escaped ones—that's the mismatch causing the wrong slice. I need to use the escaped length instead.

The fix is to calculate how many characters were stripped from the unescaped version, then use that count to slice from the end of the escaped `middle` string, since the trailing punctuation characters are always single-character entities that map one-to-one between escaped and unescaped forms.

I'm verifying that none of the trailing punctuation characters (`.,:;!`) are themselves results of HTML entity unescaping, so the character count will always match correctly between the escaped and unescaped versions.

Now I understand the issue. In the `trim_punctuation` function, after unescaping HTML entities and stripping trailing punctuation, the code incorrectly uses `len(stripped)` (from the unescaped string) to index into `middle` (the escaped string). When entities like `&lt` exist, the lengths differ, causing incorrect slicing.

Let me trace through the bug:
- `middle` = `google.com/?q=1&lt!` (19 chars)
- `middle_unescaped` = `google.com/?q=1<!` (18 chars)
- `stripped` = `google.com/?q=1<` (17 chars)
- `trail = middle[17:]` = `t!` ← WRONG (should be `!`)
- `middle = middle[:-1]` = `google.com/?q=1&lt` ← correct

The fix: use the count of stripped characters to index from the end of `middle`.
